title: Record: regular expressions in the standard library, linear unless a pattern asks to backtrack
body:
Stacked on #184: the cases write their patterns as raw literals, which #184's lexer reads. Its base is #184's branch until that merges.

## Design

The owner's answers R2 to R5 of 2026-11-01 on regular expressions, given through the question tool on #176 (comment 6560564782), are recorded in `kurz-design.md`, section 12, as a group "Regular expressions" after "Strings and lists". Each comes with what it was chosen against and its cost, as the options named them:

- R2 "In std": a `Regex` that every file sees, beside the members of a string, as C#'s base library gives it.
  - It was chosen against a first-party package, as Rust's `regex` crate stands outside its standard library, at the cost that no program could use one until the compiler builds packages.
  - Its cost: the names `Regex`, `Match` and `RegexError` are taken from every file. A pattern is code and no interchange format, so "Formats" does not reach it.
- R3 "Both, flag per pattern": a linear engine, and a backtracking one that a flag picks for one pattern.
  - It was chosen against the linear engine alone, as Rust's `regex` and .NET's `NonBacktracking`, at the cost that a pattern with a lookaround or a backreference is written another way.
  - It was chosen against backtracking alone, as .NET's default and PCRE, at the cost that a crafted text takes time exponential in its length and holds its actor's thread.
  - Its cost: two engines, and the guarantee held only where the flag is absent.
  - The guarantee is written with its mechanism and its cost (`knowledge/guarantee-needs-its-mechanism.md`). The failure it survives is any pattern and text an attacker writes. A search takes time in proportion to the pattern's size times the text's length. The mechanism is an automaton built from the pattern and run over the text once, a Pike VM with a lazy DFA where it pays, as Rust's crate runs them. The automaton is bounded by the pattern's size and the cache by a fixed capacity. The cost is no backreference and no lookaround on that engine.
- R4 "Compile time for literals": the compiler checks a literal pattern, and `Regex.New(text)` of any other string gives `Regex | RegexError` when it runs, as Rust's `Regex::new` gives a `Result`.
  - It was chosen against the check at run time alone, at the cost that a misspelt literal pattern is found when it runs and needs an `else` in top-level code.
  - It was chosen against an exception, as C#'s `RegexParseException`, at the cost that a bad pattern from input ends the actor.
  - Its cost: a parser of patterns in the compiler, an id, and a case wherever a pattern is built from a variable.
- R5 "Groups included": `re.Split(s)` puts the text of each of the pattern's groups between the pieces, as C#'s `Regex.Split` and Python's `re.split`.
  - It was chosen against the pieces alone, as Rust's `split` and Kurz's `s.Split`, at the cost that a program that wants the separators uses `Matches`.
  - Its cost: a group added for grouping alone changes the result.

Marked *(assumed)*. The answers on #176 took the product pass's readings PR1 to PR9 at their defaults:
- Positions and lengths count bytes (PR1).
- `\d`, `\w`, `\s`, `\b` and a match that ignores case take Unicode's classes from the version section 12 pins (PR2).
- `Replace` replaces every match (PR3).
- A `Regex` has members alone, with no static `Regex.IsMatch(input, pattern)` (PR4).
- `re.Match(s)` gives a `Match?` and `re.Matches(s)` a `List<Match>` (PR5), with no match that overlaps another, as C#'s `Matches` and Rust's `find_iter` give them.
- A `Match` has `Value`, `Index`, `Length` and its groups by number and by name, `null` for a group that did not take part (PR6).
- No time bound on the linear engine (PR7).
- The syntax is Rust's `regex` crate's, with `(?<name>...)` and `(?P<name>...)` both (PR8).
- No speed target in the record (PR9).
- A pattern without the flag runs on the linear engine: the reading said back with the answers.

Marked *(assumed)*, proposed with this record and not put to the owner:
- `RegexKind` is among the names every file sees. A group of a match is a `Match` too, as Rust's `Captures::get` gives one, so that no name `Group` is taken. The text of a `Regex` is its pattern.
- The flag is the named argument `backtracking: true` of `Regex.New`, a `bool`.
- Under the flag the pattern takes .NET's backreferences `\1` and `\k<name>`, its lookarounds and its atomic group, without its balancing and conditional groups. No time bound applies under the flag.
- Both engines give the same match for a pattern both take: the leftmost one, and among the alternatives at its start the first that matches.
- The automaton is bounded at 10 MiB and the lazy DFA's cache at 2 MiB. These are the defaults of Rust's `size_limit` and `dfa_size_limit`, checked 2026-11-01 in the source of `regex-automata`.
- The id `regex-invalid`. A call with a checked literal gives a `Regex` alone. A literal is checked where its flag is absent or written as `true` or `false`.
- `data RegexError(RegexKind Kind, int At)` with `enum RegexKind { Syntax, Unsupported, TooBig }`. `At` is the byte where the construct starts, as Rust's span, and 0 for `TooBig`. Its text is `syntax at 1`, as a `HexError`'s, and it holds nothing of the pattern or the text.
- The spelling `m.Group(n)` and `m.Group(name)`. `Group(0)` is the whole match. A group the pattern does not have is `null`, as Rust's `caps.get` gives `None`.
- A group that did not take part is left out of `Split`, as C#'s `Regex.Split` leaves it out.
- The replacement is read as Rust's `replace_all` reads it, where C# reads otherwise:
  - `$1a` names a group `1a`, where C# reads group 1 and an `a`;
  - a group that does not exist or did not take part gives no text, where C# keeps `$9` as it is written.

## Reference and corpus

- Chapter 16, `reference/16-regex.md`, has its own prefix, G, so that it does not meet #171's X11 at the end of chapter 15. Its rules:
  - G1 (decided, §12): the names, and a file's own declaration of one is `redeclared`;
  - G2 (decided, §12): the two engines, the guarantee, its mechanism and its cost;
  - G3 (decided, §12): a pattern's errors, at compile time and at run time;
  - G4 (assumed, §12): matching, which the pass's defaults hold;
  - G5 (decided, §12): replacing and splitting.
- Ten cases under `corpus/regex/`: `regex-redeclared`, `backtracking`, `backreference-linear` (`regex-invalid`), `invalid-literal` (`regex-invalid`), `runtime-error`, `match`, `matches`, `unicode`, `replace`, `split`.
- `reference/12-errors.md`: a row `regex-invalid` (G2, G3), and G1 in the `redeclared` row.

## Compiler

- The checker says `not supported` to `Regex`, `Match`, `RegexError` and `RegexKind` where a type, a value or a call names one. It refuses a file's own declaration of one as `redeclared`, as it does the names of #130 and #111 (`Checker.cs`: `IsRegexName`, `UnreadRegexName`).
- `CorpusTests.OutsideTheChecker` lists G1 to G5, and `compiler/README.md` lists the four names among what the checker does not read.
- `CheckerTests` gained a theory of four programs for the places a name stands, and a test of the four forms of a declaration and of a field that takes the name.
- Each change was seen red:
  - without the name in `IsDeclaredName`, `regex-redeclared.kz` and the declaration test fail;
  - without it in a function's declaration, the declaration test fails;
  - without it at a type's name, at a value's name and at a call's name, a program of the theory fails at each.

## Research findings (node B4)

None is met: no entry of `knowledge/what-developers-dislike-in-*.md` or `knowledge/what-goose-does-for-speed.md` names regular expressions, backtracking or ReDoS.

## Blast radius

19 files.
- The record: `kurz-design.md`, section 12, gains seven lines, the group and its four bullets.
- The reference: a new chapter, 16, and two rows of chapter 12 change.
- Ten new cases.
- The compiler: the checker's four names and their tests.

Nothing under `tools/`, `.github/`, `.review/`, `.claude/` or `.githooks/` changes, nor `CLAUDE.md` or `.gitattributes`. Nothing that runs a program changes: every case is `not supported` but `regex-redeclared.kz`, which the checker reads in full. No gate, tool, hook, workflow or review rule changes, so neither `knowledge/diagram-gate-map.md` nor `guides/quality-bar.md` applies.

## Checks

- `python3 tools/gates.py` on 8614cd9, the head with the fix made after the judgment (named in the acceptance comment), in the image the `gates` job runs in: 8 passed. These were self-tests (1288 cases with 1207 red proofs), tree (898 files), knowledge, reference (237 rules, 671 cases, 65 compile-error ids, 0 errors), compiler-tests (3910 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped), unicode-tables, ci-config and push-hook. `merge-checks` FAILs, since the container has no forge login. `pr-title`, `pr-breadth` and `pr-findings` were NOT RUN, with no pull request yet.
- The gates were NOT RUN on 54d1edb, the head the acceptance judge read: the run was stopped as it started, for the fix, and ran once on 8614cd9. On the host, before the judgment, the checker's and the corpus's tests passed (1844) and the reference lint gave 0 errors.
- The five mutations of the "Compiler" section were each seen red. A sixth, the name at a member's call (`Regex.New`), stayed green: the name of the target is read as a value there, which the value's place answers, so that change was dropped.
- Every regex case but `regex-redeclared.kz` gets `not supported` from the checker, so the corpus runner builds none of them: their outputs are the record's claims, which the judge computed by hand and nothing ran.
